title: Javier Bardem, Marion Cotillard and Vanessa Redgrave Join Animated Fantasy Film ‘The Turning Door’
description:
A trio of Oscar winning actors have been added to the voice cast of upcoming animated family fantasy feature “The Turning Door.”

	Javier Bardem, Ma
body:
A trio of Oscar winning actors have been added to the voice cast of upcoming animated family fantasy feature “The Turning Door.”

	Javier Bardem, Marion Cotillard and Venessa Redgrave have joined the film, written and directed by filmmaker and artist Nicholas Ashe Bateman (“The Wanting Mare”), alongside previously announced Alicia Vikander, Jamie Dornan, Jodie Turner-Smith, Bill Nighy and Gillian Anderson. Other new additions to the cast include Swedish composer Anna von Hausswolff and newcomer Pippa Kelly.
	

	The cast will perform original songs and music written by Claire Givens (“Mother Mary,” “People Museum”) and Bateman.


	Having launched the film ahead of the American Film Market in 2025, Mister Smith Entertainment will continue international sales at the upcoming TIFF market, where they will debut new footage to foreign buyers.

	In “The Turning Door,” a little girl finds a mysterious box hidden in her parent’s closet. As it grows into an open door, she falls through to another world called The Turning. There, she must embark on a grand adventure of old magic, strange creatures, new lands, alchemy, dreams and songs, all to return home and save her parents.

	The film is produced by Christine D’Souza of After Hours, Hunter Hall and Bateman of Maere Studios (“The Wanting Mare,” “An Almost Christmas Story”) and Laura Rister for Esme Grace Pictures (“Ferrari,” “The Tale”). Production is currently underway.

	“After many years of writing and dreaming about making parts for great actors, I am almost unable to express the gratitude, excitement and wonder I have for the profound gift of our cast,” said Bateman. “These are iconic artists. They bring their perspectives; their grand lives and views of the world, their immeasurable talents, towering performances, and a shared desire to make hopeful pictures for young people. Javier, Marion, Anna, Dame Vanessa Redgrave, and our dear heroine Pippa Kelly all possess a true magic which has transformed our epic.”
	

	Added Bateman: “It has been the honour of my lifetime to bring these actors — each the greatest of their generation — finally together. These are happy dreams, and the happiest: we get to hear them all sing!”

	Kharmel Cochrane cast the film. Mister Smith is handling international sales and co-repping domestic rights with After Hours.

	Bardem is repped by WME, Goodman, Genow, Schenkman, Smelkinson & Christopher, Cotillard by CAA ad Redgrave by Gavin Barker Associates and Arcierei Talent. Von Hausswolf is repped by Outro and Clinton Music, Kelly by Thompson and Borland and Bateman by Houston Costa & Danie Streisand at UTA and Granderson Des Rochers.

schema.headline: Javier Bardem, Marion Cotillard and Vanessa Redgrave Join Animated Fantasy Film ‘The Turning Door’

title: ‘Harry Potter’ Trailer: Harry Wears the Sorting Hat, Tries Quidditch and Puts on Invisibility Cloak in HBO’s TV Remake
description:
HBO’s “Harry Potter” series has released another trailer, giving a peek into the new take on the Wizarding World as it makes its way to TV.

	Newcom
body:
HBO’s “Harry Potter” series has released another trailer, giving a peek into the new take on the Wizarding World as it makes its way to TV.

	Newcomer Dominic McLaughlin stars as Harry Potter, the 11-year old wizard previously brought to life by Daniel Radcliffe. Alastair Stout and Arabella Stanton play his best friends, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger, as they enroll at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry.


	The trailer shows Harry, Ron and Hermione arriving at Hogwarts and going through the sorting ceremony, where they’re all placed in Gryffindor together. Harry meets the Hogwarts staff, including Dumbledore, Snape, McGonagall and Hagrid, while attending his magical classes, like herbology and potions, and trying out the high-flying sport of Quidditch. There’s also the mystery of the Philosopher’s Stone (aka the Sorcerer’s Stone if you’re American) that Harry, Ron and Hermione investigate. They find themselves face to face with the infamous mountain troll in the Hogwarts bathroom, playing a high-pressure game of chess and trying out the Invisibility Cloak and Mirror of Erised.
	

	The new show is a massive undertaking by HBO, which is adapting all seven of author J.K. Rowling’s books into seven seasons of TV. The first eight-episode season takes on “The Sorcerer’s Stone” and is set to release on Christmas. The show also snagged an early Season 2 renewal in May, which will follow “The Chamber of Secrets.”

	The cast includes John Lithgow as Albus Dumbledore, the headmaster of Hogwarts; Janet McTeer as Prof. McGonagall; Paapa Essiedu as Prof. Snape; Nick Frost as Hagrid; Luke Thallon as Prof. Quirrell; Paul Whitehouse as Argus Filch; Bertie Carvel as Cornelius Fudge; Johnny Flynn as Lucius Malfoy and more. Many young actors are getting their first major starts on the series as well. Lox Pratt is Draco Malfoy; Leo Earley as Seamus Finnegan; Rory Wilmot as Neville Longbottom; Gracie Cochrane as Ginny Weasley; and Elijah Oshin as Dean Thomas.
	

	HBO dropped a first-look image on March 24 that showed McLaughlin as Harry in Gryffindor robes. He’s walking up to the Quidditch pitch on the Hogwarts school grounds, surrounded by other students in their school clothes. That was later followed by a full trailer, which revealed the new looks at Ron, Hermione, Dumbledore, Snape and other fan-favorite characters.

	Watch the trailer below.

title: ‘I’m Hoping to See Sydney Sweeney’: Meet the Superfans Who Camp Out All Night for Celebrity Sightings at Venice Film Festival
description: It’s 11:30 p.m. on Tuesday, and 19-year-old Delsina Desanctes is standing outside the Palazzo de Cinema — the iconic venue where the Venice Film Fes
body:
It’s 11:30 p.m. on Tuesday, and 19-year-old Delsina Desanctes is standing outside the Palazzo de Cinema — the iconic venue where the Venice Film Festival takes place — surrounded by umbrellas, suitcases, sleeping bags and even a tent.

	“I’m hoping to see Sydney Sweeney, Kendall Jenner and Jonathan Bailey,” says Desanctes, who traveled to Lido from Rome. (None of them are at the fest for movies; they’re attending as brand ambassadors for Armani.)
	

	It’s a full 24 hours before anyone famous will walk the red carpet, but that hasn’t stopped Venice superfans from camping out a day early. Every film festival has its die-hards who gather hours in advance to catch a glimpse at their favorite celebrities and share the bragging rights on Instagram and TikTok. But at Venice, it’s an all-night affair. Along with the umbrellas to block the sun, people are equipped with mosquito repellant, water bottles, portable phone chargers and tripods. If you squint, it almost looks like camp grounds at Burning Man or Coachella (without the dust).


	Desanctes isn’t fazed by the brutal heat or hours of waiting around. This is her seventh year in the thick of the action, and she’s gotten good at passing the time. In fact, she’s not even all that interested in the stars. She’s saving a spot for her celebrity-obsessed best friend, who is back at their hotel taking a disco nap before the fun begins.



	

					Delsina Desanctes is saving a spot for her celebrity-obsessed best friend
	



	“I smoke. I love talking to people, so the time passes,” Desanctes says. “I didn’t eat or drink all day today, so tomorrow I’m going to reset. It’s crazy, but it’s the only time of year I’m going to do that.”
	

	Michele, a 29-year-old Italian who has attended the festival for the past decade, took off work so he could get to the Palazzo by 6 p.m. on Tuesday. It’s a lot of effort, sure, but he learned the hard way that showing up any later meant he’d get a lame placement on the carpet. If you don’t have a decent view of the action, you certainly won’t be able to score any autographs or selfies.

	“Last year, I arrived at 9 p.m. the day before, and it was too late. I was on the last part of the red carpet,” he says. “If I got here tomorrow, I’d be in the third or fourth row.”

	That’s a problem, he says, because the crowd tends to erupt into a frenzy when A-listers finally descend on the red carpet. “Everyone, at least the first time they’re here, makes some mistakes. You push people a little. I’ve done it as well. It’s like a battle royale,” says Michele. “I’m not proud of it, but this year I’m trying to change and redeem myself.”

	George Clooney, who is being honored with a life achievement award, as well as the cast of Danny Boyle’s Rupert Murdoch drama “Ink,” including Jack O’Connell, Claire Foy and Guy Pearce, are among the bold-face names who will attend the opening night festivities. Michele wants to meet Boyle, his favorite director, but he’s prepared to be disappointed.

	“It’s a roll of the dice,” Michele says. “Some of them are very kind. It’s not their fault if they don’t take an autograph or selfie with every person on the red carpet. They have a schedule.”

	Venice’s artistic director Alberto Barbera, who happened to be walking by the Palazzo de Cinema on Tuesday night as people were already staking out the grounds, admitted he doesn’t know what to make of the unusual scene.

	“I can’t believe they’re so crazy to stay for two days,” Barbera says. “Of course, it’s weird. But at the same time, they show there’s a real passion. The fact that they put themselves in such a situation, not caring about the fatigue, not caring if they eat, it’s impressive.”

	Local police officers, meanwhile, say they can’t comprehend the appeal of sleeping on the ground in the name of capturing a few photos and videos. And it’s apparently illegal in Venice for tourists who sit, lay down or camp in public areas, with fines ranging from €200 to €350, according to two officials who declined to be named. But they aren’t trying to disrupt the fun.
	

	“We are not fining them. If it were a normal day, we would take them away from there and give them a warning that they must stay out of the city center for two days,” says one police officer. “As a Venetian, I don’t understand it.”



	

					Camping out is bonding for mother and daughter Samantha Sandri and Bianca Baccolini
	



	The all-nighter has become an annual event for Bianca Baccolini, 20, and her mom, Samantha Sandri, of Bologna. They returned to the sidewalk, having captured cherished videos in years prior of Brad Pitt, Clooney and Lady Gaga. This time around, they were joined by six friends — another parent and kids ranging from 14 to 21 years old — whom they met at the 2025 festival.

	“It’s a beautiful experience,” says Baccolini, who hopes to snag pictures of Clooney (again), Orlando Bloom and Robert Pattinson. Her mom describes the adventure as “magic.”  

	“The filmmakers and actors come to see you, and they’re friendly,” Sandri says. “And my daughter and I get to spend time together.”

schema.headline: ‘I’m Hoping to See Sydney Sweeney’: Meet the Superfans Who Camp Out All Night for Celebrity Sightings at Venice Film Festival

title: ‘My Notes on Mars’ Review: Mackenzie Davis and Rupert Friend Star in an Imperfect Breakdown of Marriage and Memory
description: A relationship drama verging on sci-fi, Lili Horvát’s “My Notes On Mars” begins with an intriguing premise that eventually loses steam. It follows t
body:
A relationship drama verging on sci-fi, Lili Horvát’s “My Notes On Mars” begins with an intriguing premise that eventually loses steam. It follows the disappearance of an American astrophysicist in the Hungarian mountains who mysteriously returns to her husband on the day of her own memorial. With no memory of who she is or where she’s been, all she’s left with is a single-minded obsession to destroy her research. The film is downright Tarkovskian for its initial hour, unspooling through eerie abstractions that heighten its lingering domestic turmoil. However, its growing mysteries nudge it, paradoxically, toward the literal, leaving it with few places to go.
	

	The opening images find Margot Fogle (Mackenzie Davis) floating in the outdoor pool of her new, rural homestead just outside Budapest. The sound drowns out as the water covers her ears; as she shuts her eyes, we’re transported — perhaps through her imagination — further and further away from her life on Earth, all the way to Mars’ surface, right down to a microscopic level where strange shapes emerge. This kaleidoscopic introduction recalls the work of Percival Lowell, a 19th-century astronomer name-dropped in passing, who claimed to have discovered advanced irrigation on the red planet by way of telescopic observation. Sadly, this turned out to be a reflection of the blood vessels in his retina.


	So too does “My Notes On Mars” gaze at the sky in order to look inward, amidst frequent talk of humanity escaping its earthbound confines to colonize the heavens. Margot has left her field, and has moved to Hungary with her equestrian husband Sam (Rupert Friend), an uprooting that manifests as quiet disconnects between them. She just can’t seem to make the commitments demanded of her (usually, Sam’s robust social gatherings) and she becomes further distracted when inspiration strikes, taking copious mathematical notes on her hand. She discovered something vital about Mars’ terrain, but Sam is fed up with the growing chasm between them. Margot’s sudden academic spark leads to sleepless nights, and thus, exhaustion on the mountainous hike she reluctantly agrees to, if only to satiate Sam’s frustrations. This is the last he sees of her — that is, until her unexplained homecoming two months later.  
	

	There’s something alluringly alien-esque about Davis’ body language here, an intentional stiltedness and curiosity as Margot takes in the world anew, though not before Sam passes out at the sight of her. What follows is, at first, a deft examination of relationships under quiet stress, where the barely hidden metaphor coheres through a tale of a husband who no longer knows his wife, a wife who no longer knows herself and a society looking to escape its own mundane confines. The only things Margot knows for sure is that she needs to burn her notebook, lest the secrets of Mars be uncovered. That and the fact that she’s attracted to a young employee at a Hungarian observatory, the enthusiastic Alex (Atanáz Babinchak), whom she met just once, as they discussed their common interest in the stars.

	Horvát and cinematographer Róbert Maly wrap the story’s gradual unveiling in a curious haze — an intimate glow complemented by Gábor Keresztes’s shimmering score, which resembles the quieter moments of “Interstellar.” However, there’s only so long the film can sustain its inviting double meanings before it finds the need to wheel-spin. Davis is tremendous in the role, especially when saddled with primal urges connected to sound and smell, forcing the question of just who (or what) she has become. However, her performance soon takes on a more grounded, childlike cadence, which roots the supposedly amnesiac Margot a little too firmly within the literal, especially for a tale whose poetry lies in its uncanniness. Similarly, Sam’s frustrations — which Friend embodies through suppressed agitation — seldom evolve as the situation is prolonged, and new information about the disappearance changes little about the plot.

	Granted, the central symbolism is as much about grieving a relationship as it is about the denial of that grief. Its repetition is, therefore, not without its reasons, but it yields emotional plateaus, and a destination too emotionally vague to elicit a response. Once you’ve picked up on what the story is about, there’s no meaningful metamorphosis to keep you hooked. Despite some dazzling aesthetic confidence, “My Notes On Mars” plays the same dramatic beats ad nauseam until things begins to stagnate. At the very least, that’s a fitting outcome for a film about a marriage running its course.

schema.headline: ‘My Notes on Mars’ Review: Mackenzie Davis and Rupert Friend Star in an Imperfect Breakdown of Marriage and Memory

title: ‘Black Book 2,’ ‘I’m Coming for You’ Headline Buzzy Slate of African Works in Progress at Inaugural TIFF Market (EXCLUSIVE)
description: CANEX Creations Inc., the pan-African investment platform behind films such as the buzzy Cannes premiere “Clarissa,” has unveiled a slate of works i
body:
CANEX Creations Inc., the pan-African investment platform behind films such as the buzzy Cannes premiere “Clarissa,” has unveiled a slate of works in progress that it will be screening for prospective buyers at the inaugural TIFF: The Market. Among them are director Editi Effiong’s sequel to his breakout Netflix hit “Black Book” and the fiction debut of Rotterdam-winning filmmaker Cyrielle Raingou (“Le Spectre de Boko Haram”).
	

	The market screenings, which will take place at 11 a.m. on Sept. 12 at TIFF Lightbox Cinema 7, are part of an ambitious program of events hosted by CANEX Creations Inc. across the week-long event, which runs Sept. 10–16. The subsidiary of the African Export-Import Bank’s (Afreximbank) equity-investment arm is an official partner of TIFF: The Market.

	Speaking to Variety ahead of this year’s event, CANEX Creations Inc. CEO Osahon Akpata noted that the six titles were selected by an independent jury precisely for their market potential.


	“We are particularly proud that these projects were selected by an independent international jury with deep experience across production, distribution, international sales, festivals and African and global film markets,” said Akpata.

	“African cinema is gaining greater visibility on the world’s leading festival stages, with compelling work emerging from an increasingly broad range of countries,” he continued. “Our objective is to help translate that creative momentum into commercial opportunity by putting market-ready projects in front of the buyers, distributors and financiers who can take them to global audiences.”
	

	The slate includes “The Black Book 2: Old Scores,” director Editi Effiong’s follow-up to the 2023 revenge thriller that hit No. 3 on Netflix’s global charts and cracked the top 10 in 69 countries, racking up more than 20 million views worldwide. The sequel sees Paul Edima returning to continue his fight against the corrupt system that destroyed his family

	Also screening for key North American acquisition and distribution executives is “I’m Coming for You” (pictured), the first fiction feature by Cameroonian filmmaker Cyrielle Raingou, who won the top prize at the Rotterdam Film Festival in 2023 for her documentary “Le Spectre de Boko Haram.” The film is a story about motherhood, survival and resistance that follows a young woman who’s been banished from her community.

	Other titles on the slate include “Last Weekend in October,” a documentary by Nigerian filmmaker Nosarieme Garrick set during Lagos Fashion Week; “Dear Ajayi,” a family drama by Damilola Orimogunje that marks the first Nigerian film to screen in the Venice Film Festival’s Venice Days strand; “Not God’s Plan,” a new drama from South African writer-director Reabetswe Moeti-Vogt; and “The Motorcycle Smuggler,” the latest from Cameroon’s Arice Siapi. More details about all six projects can be found below.

	In addition to those films, CANEX Creations will host a buyers screening of “Muganga – The One Who Treats,” the advocacy-driven drama inspired by the true story of Nobel Peace Prize laureate Dr. Denis Mukwege, which is directed by Marie-Hélène Roux and co-produced by Angelina Jolie. The screening, which takes place at 9:45 p.m. on Sept. 11 at the John Bassett Theater, will be followed by a conversation with Mukwege and actors David Oyelowo and Danai Gurira, moderated by British writer and broadcaster Afua Hirsch.

	Here’s a rundown of the six WIP:

	Last Weekend in OctoberDirector: Nosarieme GarrickProducers: Chioma Onyenwe, Mary-Ann EziekweSynopsis: Set against the competitive world of Lagos Fashion Week, “Last Weekend in October” follows three emerging designers fighting for the visibility that could transform their careers. Through their experiences, the documentary explores ambition, identity and the often unseen forces that determine who gets noticed, and who gets left behind, in Nigeria’s fashion industry.
	

	I’m Coming for You (Pour toi je reviendrai)Director: Cyrielle RaingouProducers: Cyrielle Raingou, Jean-Marie GigonSynopsis: In the Sahel, Kaltoumi, a young mother, is banished from her community and separated from her baby after being accused of trading with terrorists. Determined to recover her child, she sets out on a journey that brings her into contact with a group of women living on the margins, in a story about motherhood, survival and resistance to both terrorism and patriarchal control.

	Dear AjayiDirector: Damilola OrimogunjeProducers: Damilola Orimogunje, Ajah Enene-Orimogunje, Bose OshinSynopsis: Set in southwestern Nigeria in the 1990s, “Dear Ajayi” follows estranged sisters Ade and Titi as they are brought back together to care for their ailing mother. As old tensions resurface, the sisters must confront their very different ideas about faith, ambition and responsibility, as well as the grief and complicated bonds that hold their family together.

	Not God’s PlanDirector: Reabetswe Moeti-VogtProducers: Reabetswe Moeti-Vogt, Zoe RamushuSynopsis: After receiving what he believes is a terminal diagnosis, lifelong bachelor Gilbert leaves Johannesburg and returns to the rural village he once fled, determined to make amends with the women he hurt and put his affairs in order. But when he discovers that he misunderstood his diagnosis, the journey has already changed him, reconnecting him with family, love and the home he left behind.

	The Motorcycle SmugglerDirector: Arice SiapiProducers: Martinel Nemalieu, Eléonore BoissinotSynopsis: Bana, a former motorcycle smuggler turned traditional musician, has left the dangerous trade behind. But after his father’s death leaves him responsible for his family, he agrees to make one final smuggling journey to finance a new album, returning to the perilous routes and former companions he had hoped to leave behind.

	The Black Book 2: Old ScoresDirector: Editi EffiongProducers: Editi Effiong, Nicky Weinstock, Mimi BartelsSynopsis: Paul Edima returns in the sequel to “The Black Book,” continuing his fight against the corrupt system that destroyed his family. As old enemies and unfinished business resurface, Paul is drawn deeper into a struggle for justice and redemption against a wider network of corruption and abuse of power in contemporary Nigeria.

title: How ‘The Challenge’ Turned Thailand’s Heat and Streets Into Part of the Competition
description:
T.J. Lavin has hosted “The Challenge” across the globe, but Thailand left an impression that outlasted the shoot.

	“It was one of the most incredib
body:
T.J. Lavin has hosted “The Challenge” across the globe, but Thailand left an impression that outlasted the shoot.

	“It was one of the most incredible and fun places that I’ve ever been. I absolutely loved it. Not to mention, foot massages on the daily were amazing. The people are the sweetest in the world for sure,” he tells Variety. Away from the cameras, he found a new favorite mode of transport. “I had no idea that we never needed a car in Thailand. Scooters are my way of traveling, specifically by motor scooter. Absolutely love them,” he says.
	

	That affection for the country runs through Season 42, now airing on Paramount+ following its MTV debut. The season brings back the franchise’s ‘Cutthroat’ format, splitting 24 competitors into three teams battling for a share of $500,000. For executive producer Justin Booth, the return to Thailand was less about scenery and more about what the country’s crews and locations made possible. “We came back to Thailand for a few reasons, but primarily because of the strength of the local production staff and the opportunity to explore locations we hadn’t worked in before,” he tells Variety. Filming across Bangkok, Pattaya and the wider Chonburi region, he adds, “gave us the ability to maximize our production value in ways we couldn’t have done elsewhere.”


	That production value, Booth says, comes down to talent. “Thailand has some of the most professional and polished art department personnel anywhere in the world, and you’re able to access that level of talent at a better price. That allows us to maximize what we put on screen,” he says. He rates the country’s infrastructure above most places the show has filmed. “The local production support, the personnel, and the access are all fantastic, and I’d say they’re better than what you find in most places around the world,” he says.
	

	Thailand didn’t just sit in the frame, either. Lavin says the heat and humidity became part of the competition itself. “The humidity really added to the physical demands. The air can feel so thick at times that even some of the easiest tasks become difficult, let alone a serious Challenge,” he says, pointing to one task in particular as a season standout: “The very first Challenge that we did where they had to run through the streets was filmed in downtown Bangkok. I think that made it really cool.”

	Booth traces some of that texture to how reality television engages with a location differently than scripted work does. When the cast heads into a city or town, he says, “they’re experiencing that location in a way that’s very similar to what a visitor might experience,” a dynamic he sees as distinct from how scripted productions typically present a destination.

	Reviving ‘Cutthroat’, last used by the franchise in 2009, changes how contestants have to play. “It was a huge success when we did it in 2009, and we felt like this was the right time to bring it back. We had the right cast, and the format felt right for this particular season,” Booth says. Season 42 marks a shift from the paired and individual competition of recent seasons, he notes, back toward a team dynamic the franchise hasn’t explored in years – the dynamic he says viewers should watch closest as the season unfolds.

	Lavin says the adjustment to team play came easier to some than others. “I think everyone really did well in their teams. The veterans really know how to play. So they knew what they had to do, and the rookies didn’t know any different, so they didn’t have to adjust,” he says. He’s just as bullish on the rookie class itself. “All of the rookies not only have great gameplay, but they also have strong performances. I think you’ll be very surprised by the veterans for a reason. They know what to do and how to do it.”

	Without spoiling what’s ahead, both men are teasing more to come. Lavin points to a franchise staple as the moment worth circling. “Every season has a mini final, and this one is no exception. If I were a viewer, that’s something I’d be looking forward to,” he says. He’s cagier about the rest, but not by much. “I have a really good feeling about this season because everything that’s happened could have been produced. It was so good, but it wasn’t. I have a feeling that we are gonna have some heated rivalries in the future,” he says.
	

	Both also see Thailand’s presence on screen as more than production logistics. Lavin thinks the show can move viewers to book flights. “I definitely think people want to travel where they see on television and/or on social media. I think it has a lot to do with where they decide to go. Thailand is one of the most beautiful places in the world,” he says.

	Neither is done with the country yet. Booth confirms the franchise would return without hesitation, citing unfinished business with the destination. “We’d love to come back to Thailand. We’ve always enjoyed our time there and the productions we’ve done there. Even after this season, there are still so many parts of the country we haven’t explored, and we’d love the opportunity to see what else Thailand has to offer,” he says.

title: Danny Boyle Celebrated at Variety’s Venice Pre-Opening Party as ‘Ink’ Star Jack O’Connell Praises His Ability to ‘Take Us Inside a World’
description: Danny Boyle was celebrated with Variety’s Creative Impact in Directing Award on Monday during a Venice Film Festival pre-opening night party at the
body:
Danny Boyle was celebrated with Variety’s Creative Impact in Directing Award on Monday during a Venice Film Festival pre-opening night party at the poolside terrace of the Hotel Excelsior.

	The Oscar-winning British filmmaker is set to open the festival on Wednesday night with “Ink,” a juicy exposé of how British tabloid The Sun propelled Rupert Murdoch’s rise to right-wing media baron. In his speech, Boyle praised Venice chief Alberto Barbera for his “courage” in choosing “Ink” as opener. 
	

	“When Alberto rang up to say that this film was going to open the Venice Film Festival, I thought he was insane,” Boyle said, adding that “Ink” is “the oddest film that’s ever opened Venice.”


	“There are directors who are able to utilize their craft to present us a world. Then there are directors like Danny Boyle, who know how to take us inside a world,” said Jack O’Connell, who stars in “Ink” as The Sun editor Larry Lamb, in presenting the award to Boyle.

	“Danny has always had a remarkable and unique instinct for capturing the mood of Britain and its people, from directing ‘Trainspotting’ to staging the opening ceremony of the London Olympics, he has repeatedly found ways to reflect something essential about the country at a particular moment in time,” O’Connell added.

	Also on hand to celebrate Boyle were O’Connell’s “Ink” co-stars Claire Foy and Guy Pearce.



	

	



	In his speech, Barbera said how pleased he was that, after a one-year hiatus, Variety’s pre-opening party was back since it has become “an integral part of the festival experience.”

	“Tonight cocktail’s is much more than a social gathering. It’s a chance to celebrate cinema, but also the people who make it possible,” Barbera said. “Venice is about to become once again one of the great meeting places of world cinema; a unique crossroads bringing together directors, actors, producers, distributors, journalists, industry professionals, and of course, film lovers.”
	

	He added, “Intense days lie ahead of us. Days filled with screenings, meetings, press conferences, discussion, discoveries, emotion, and, inevitably, a few surprises. Good surprises, I hope, of course.”

	Variety co-editor-in-chief Ramin Setoodeh pointed out that Venice is “really the official launch of awards season. I can’t wait to see all the great movies that are going to be playing here!”

	Also in attendance were Venice jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal, spotted chatting away with Boyle; directors Akinola Davies Jr. and Carolina Cavalli; Italian marketing guru and film festivals specialist Tiziana Rocca, who co-hosted the party; and lots of industry heavyweights including Italy’s RAI Cinema chief Paolo Del Brocco, producer Michael Ellenberg and actor, director and producer Maria Soccor.



	

	



	The 83rd edition of Venice will run Sept. 2-12.

schema.headline: Danny Boyle Celebrated at Variety’s Venice Pre-Opening Party as ‘Ink’ Star Jack O’Connell Praises His Ability to ‘Take Us Inside a World’

title: Inde Navarrette Sets Best Actress Oscar Campaign for ‘Obsession’ as Focus Features Mounts Full Awards Push (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Will the Oscars love Inde Navarrette, like “a love only the branch of a willow tree could conjure?”

	Variety can exclusively confirm that Navarrett
body:
Will the Oscars love Inde Navarrette, like “a love only the branch of a willow tree could conjure?”

	Variety can exclusively confirm that Navarrette will campaign in the best actress category this coming awards season for her breakout turn in Curry Barker’s box office smash “Obsession,” headlining a wide-ranging effort from Focus Features that will seek recognition across nearly every category the film is eligible to enter.
	

	It is a seismic full-court press studios reserve for a title they believe can go the distance. Alongside Navarrette, the distributor plans to campaign Barker as a rare triple threat in best director, original screenplay and film editing, the same three categories Sean Baker swept for his best picture winner “Anora” (which he also took alongside one more as producer). It is a combination of above-the-line and below-the-line recognition that positions him as one of the season’s marquee multi-hyphenate stories.


	Navarrette’s place in the best actress gives the campaign its center of gravity to get through the next several months. Studios build best picture runs around a face and a narrative, and Focus is betting that a breakout turn is the engine that pulls the rest of the slate into the race. The studio will also be steering the anticipated drama “Elsinore” starring Andrew Scott, the remake of “Sense and Sensibility” with Daisy Edgar-Jones and another entry from a horror master, Robert Eggers’ “Werwulf.”

	The low-budget horror-romance has grossed more than $505.6 million worldwide against a slim $750,000 production budget.
	

	One consequential decision facing “Obsession” still remains unsettled: its Golden Globes campaign. Focus and the filmmakers have yet to decide (or confirm) whether “Obsession” will seek consideration in the drama or the musical or comedy race. That playbook is not new, as seen in 2017 with Jordan Peele’s horror hit “Get Out” competing as a comedy at the Globes. The movie went on to land four Academy Award nominations, including best picture, best director for Peele and best actor for Daniel Kaluuya, and it won best original screenplay.

	For now, the call remains open. But if the musical or comedy route holds, expect “Obsession” to lean into the “Get Out” comparison rather than run from it.

	Below is the complete list of categories Focus Features intends to submit this season.



	

					OBSESSION, from left: Inde Navarrette, Michael Johnston, 2025. © Focus Features / Courtesy Everett Collection
									©Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection
	




Best Picture 
Best Director — Curry Barker
Best Actress — Inde Navarrette
Best Actor — Michael Johnston
Best Supporting Actor — Cooper Tomlinson
Best Supporting Actress — Megan Lawless
Best Supporting Actor — Andy Richter
Original Screenplay — Curry Barker
Film Editing — Curry Barker
Cinematography — Taylor Clemons
Original Score — Rock Burwell
Casting — Skyler Zurn
Sound — YJ Gold (production sound mixer) and Ben Zarai (supervising sound editor, rerecording mixer)
Makeup and Hairstyling — Allie Shehorn (makeup and hair department head)
Production Design — Vivian Gray

title: David Byrne’s Hollywood Bowl Shows Put a Seal on One of the Greatest Rock Tours of All Time: Concert Review
description:
Well, Brady Corbet has got his work cut out for him.

	That was one of the first thoughts that came to mind soon after David Byrne and company took
body:
Well, Brady Corbet has got his work cut out for him.

	That was one of the first thoughts that came to mind soon after David Byrne and company took the stage for the first of two shows at the Hollywood Bowl this weekend. It stemmed from an announcement having come out just one day earlier that Corbet, the director of “The Brutalist,” had already shot shows along Byrne’s long-running tour, in 70mm, for the purposes of a feature film. The proper first response to that news was delight, that one of the most striking tours of all time, now coming to a close, was going to be captured for posterity by a visually inventive filmmaker. And the inevitable second response should have been: Yes, but how can he?
	

	At the Bowl, you might have been tempted to make a fleeting mental game out of how a show with this many moving parts — which is to say, constantly moving humans — might be wrassled to the ground for a satisfying screen experience. But ultimately that was too distracting a thought experiment to pursue for very long when, before your eyes, you had one of the greatest shows on earth, and what surely has felt to everyone who has seen it across 140 or so dates like a you had to be there experience. Viewers have come away from the “Who Is the Sky?” shows over the past year like glassy-eyed cultists, suddenly feeling, as corny as it sounds, like it’s good to be alive. And to cut off one letter to reduce that thought into Pollstar terms: It’s good to be live.


	For anyone who hasn’t been caught up on the conceptual conceits of this particular tour, a thumbnail description goes something like: “‘American Utopia,’ but better.” (Sorry, Spike Lee, helmer of the previous tour’s pretty good film rendering.) Byrne had started reinventing the concert wheel a long time ago, in the “Stop Making Sense” days, but he really gave things a revolutionary twist with the 2018 tour that rethought how musicians could be made to be seen behave on stage, essentially as sort of free-range chickens, untethered to any visible wires or technology or anything except adherence to brilliant choreography. But “American Utopia” was a monochrome affair, all grey suits and static, beaded curtains, which was a decent enough way of framing the players. “Who Is the Sky?” is the expansion of that idea into stupendous Technicolor, using everything from elaborate LED backdrops and floorings to glow-in-the-dark sneakers to create an expansive sense of “moving out in all directions,” to quote “And She Was.” (Along with occasional pauses for the master of ceremonies to stop and give his TED talk.)
	



	

					HB26 – David Byrne: Who Is The Sky? – Hollywood Bowl – August 28, 2026
									Timothy Norris/Los Angeles Philh
	



	For these Bowl shows, Byrne — or somebody — had the ingenious idea to have the concerts opened by the USC Trojan Marching Band, who managed to squeeze a freshly minted Dolly Parton tribute into their hits medley. (There was a little bit of booing, apparently from UCLA partialists, when they first appeared, but look, Bruins, ‘SC earned lifetime rights to this sort of thing by having been booked for “Tusk,” which is still the climax of their set. Life and Lyndsey Buckingham aren’t fair that way.) The Trojans, who took up too much floor space on the Bowl stage to do any marching, per se, were themselves preceded by Stroll Groove, a small dance troupe that specializes in the slightly nostalgic art of stepping. Something both these openers have in common is a sense of self-containment, that you could set them down in any amphitheater or park and they could do their thing, even if Byrne’s production is too high-tech to really be that movable a feast.

	But in some sense, booking the USC band was a sly way of giving away the magic trick, almost. Byrne and his dozen musicians and dancers are a marching band, too, in all of their glorious mobility and wirelessness. There is no quick and easy way to summarize exactly what it is this talented crew is doing, when that is constantly changing, but it always involves constant changes in where people are located on stage and what they’re up to, and even whether they are moving together in close formation or allowed to be funky and free for a few moments before the choreography tightens up again. Even the instrumentation is constantly shifting, and there’s a constant sense of happy disbelief that the full arrangements we’re hearing are actually emanating from the relatively few dancing musicians who are interacting with the singer-hoofers. (If we can count on anybody not to cheat on that, it’s probably Byrne.) It’s as if every instrument you ever imagined was somehow adapted into being the equivalent of a key-tar. But, obviously, marching band and first-line directors have been dealing with these issues since time memorial, so Byrne is innovating as part of a fine tradition.



	

					HB26 – David Byrne: Who Is The Sky? – Hollywood Bowl – August 28, 2026
									Timothy Norris/Los Angeles Philh
	



	Not enough can be said in praise of how, in a world where LED screens are ubiquitous on every big tour, Byrne’s design is especailly well-thought-through. We can add the caveat here that the Dolby Theatre down the street in Hollywood, where this show played last November, was the ideal size for this production, where the screens provided a more immersive experience. At the Bowl, from a distance, even screens that fill up two-thirds of the width of the stage can feel postage stamp-sized. But it was still spectacle enough for 17,500 people, whatever the production was scaled for originally.
	

	One of the most imaginative wrinkles in the staging is one the average viewer might not even be noticing, or at least thinking much about. Among the 13 people on stage, not once does anyone ever enter from stage left or stage right, which would be a major distraction, given how frequently these slippery people are coming in or out. Rather, they are making these transitions via the spaces separating the central LED panel from the left and right screens. (There are backdrop panels between the panels, to create a fairly seamless widescreen effect most of the time, or about as seamless as the original three-panel Cinerama ever was.) The show opens with Byrne singing the Talking Heads classic “Heaven” accompanied by only three other musicians — two string players and a keyboardist — in an echo of how the “Stop Making Sense” film portrayed the ensemble starting out small and then getting bigger, much bigger. But here, conversely, the nearly invisible entrances and exits seem designed not to leave you consciously thinking about how many of the participants are or aren’t on stage at a given time. You just know that, quickly, it comes to be a lot. And somehow, the ensemble comes to intuitively feel like some kind of wildly friendly vision of our shared humanity — their uniform orange jumpsuits symbolizing our commonality, even as the cast’s movement and playing exemplified our rich differences.



	

					HB26 – David Byrne: Who Is The Sky? – Hollywood Bowl – August 28, 2026
									Timothy Norris/Los Angeles Philharmonic
	



	That description may sound lofty for what is, after all, a rock ‘n’ roll show. But Byrne has a way of putting you in that heady space. At the conclusion of “Heaven,” he and the initially small crew of musicians took a time out to just stand in front of the still image of earth, taken from outer space, and let everyone consider our island home from a distance for a minute. “There she is,” he said. “Our heaven. As seen on TV. The only one we have.” He could wax on about the natural order of things, and our unnatural response to it. Introducing another song later on, Byrne talked about animals and asked, “Who’s to say that they’re not feeling something similar inside to what we feel? We don’t know. This separation between us and nature, animals and plants and everything else began a long time ago, but it really kicked into gear only a few hundred years ago, and we’ve been living with the consequences ever since. The good news is it doesn’t have to be that way forever.”And then he and the band performed “What Humans Do,”with an overhead screen showing footage of the group playing the song with animal masks on.
	

	There were, of course, numbers that emphasized the world-scrutinizing whimsy he has brought to much of his material over the past 50 years. “I Met the Buddha at a Downtown Party” is a song with a rather self-explanatory title, which didn’t stop Byrne from prefacing it with a short, funny lecture about different ways the Buddha has been portrayed throughout history, including one where “he was given a retractable penis. Now we’re getting somewhere! Now, maybe half of you in the audience will say, ‘What’s so special about that? I’ve got one of those.’ But his might have been special.” He even put up a slide show, with “some depictions (that) have him looking like a young, handsome monk with a kind of bun hairdo and extraordinarily large ears. Other depictions have him (as) a rather more corpulent fellow with Robert Smith’s makeup.” Sure enough, the accompanying illo got a laugh. Divine figures like their pastries and pancake mascara, too, just like us new-wave veterans.

	Byrne has a part of the show each evening, apparently, in which he catches everyone up on what he did in town that day, photo montage included. On Friday, he said, with the band having taken the train up from San Diego, as touring rockers are wont to do (?), he then “biked from Union Station to our hotel in West Hollywood, which was kind of a crazy thing to do, but I did it. And I did it so I could take some pictures. Here we go.” He put up pics from Grand Central Market — “things to take home, things to consume on the premises,” he remarked, which sounded like a line from an early Talking Heads song. He showed geometric patterns he enjoyed on a concrete restraining wall: “Los Angeles works very hard to constrain nature — keep nature from burning the city down, washing the city away, having the city roll down the hill.” And, then, a famous east Hollywood haunt. “Now we’re getting somewhere, right? Everybody’s been to Jumbo’s Clown Room. Oh, boy. I’m not gonna say anything about this place that features these lovely Thai ladies. But yes… If you’re looking to meet a clown, if that’s your thing, this is the place to go.”

	But for all those stand-up routine elements, he was mostly serious. Byrne introduced “When We Are Singing” with clips of Italians singing on their balconies during quarantine — “they happened to have really nice voices” — on Liberation Day, the “day they celebrate their freedom from fascism.” That was as political as it got. He prefaced “Everybody’s Coming to My House,” the first encore number, with a notation that his current arrangement of the song is borrowed from the Abyssinian Baptist Church in Harlem, and he said he realized, “Now I know what this song is about… Some years ago, when the pandemic was easing up, these outdoor restaurants started opening here and there, and I remember riding around on my bike downtown New York, and I heard a sound. It sounded familiar, but I couldn’t quite place it. Wasn’t quite sure what it was. So I stopped my bike in the middle of the street, got out, listened, and I realized, ‘Oh, it’s people.’ People talking to one another. It had been a while. Whoo! And I thought, ‘Despite all our differences, despite all the craziness, people love being with other people.'”
	

	David Byrne, the one-time psycho-killer channeler who is really just a person who loves people, trying to expand the company of the luckiest people of all.

	Bicycling every day, by the way, seems to have served him well. The 74-year-old singer-songwriter is in visibly great shape, keeping up with the agility of his dancer-musician companions at every step, every sway and every sudden crouch. His voice sounds exactly as it did five decades ago… included the patented high-pitched cries of “Thank you” that we wondered if they were affectations when we heard them on bootlets 50 years ago. (They weren’t; Byrne has always been a more earnest guy than we first imagined.) There’s hardly anything happening on stage that he isn’t a direct and equal participant in, without ever overshadowing anyone in his visual orbit… all the way down to the subtle line-dancing homage with thumbs hooked into pockets in the surprisingly country flavored-“Independence Day.”

	Some of the visuals that remain in memory: The way his and the other participants’ names appear in the cosmos on screen overhead during one number, corresponding to exactly where they are moving around on the stage below, as if they were stars moving to their own beat through the constellations. The way that “Nothing but Flowers” is backdropped with a liminal space before the cornfield suddenly takes over civilization at the end. The 360 views of his real-life New York high-rise living space during “My Apartment Is My Friend” (a completely unironic ode to how the right home can be your bestie). The mock-drone overhead elation of “And She Was” (introduced with an amusing story about how it was inspired by Byrne’s acid-dropping childhood friend). But sometimes, the imagery didn’t need to be elaborate. The crew’s glowing-in-the-dark blue sneakers, set against a pure orange backdrop, was as striking and weirdly satisfying a visual as anything put on stage or screen during the evening.

	“We’re only tourists in this life / Only tourists, but the view is nice,” he sang during the penultimate number, before the house inevitably got burned down for the climax. With Byrne as one of the best tour guides we could ever get, the view at the Hollywood Bowl had never been better — sights and sounds that feel like they’re rearranged your molecules, in some way that you hope lasts more than just a couple post-euphoric days.
	

	After about 40 shows last year and 90 more this year, the “Who Is the Sky?” tour will very shortly draw to a close after a few dates in Mexico and a closing night at Forest Hills Stadium in Queens Sept. 19. As for its possible eternal life, if Corbet manages to get even 60% of what this show felt like as well as looked and sounded like onto a 70mm screen, that might be good enough.

title: Nimesh Patel’s Netflix Special ‘Buy the Dip’ Sets September Release (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Nimesh Patel‘s Netflix special has been given a title and release date.

	“Buy the Dip,” an hour of stand-up comedy, will debut on the streamer on S
body:
Nimesh Patel‘s Netflix special has been given a title and release date.

	“Buy the Dip,” an hour of stand-up comedy, will debut on the streamer on Sept. 22. In what’s described as a “no-punches-pulled special,” Patel covers the “absurdity of parenting, the insanity of his Indian family and the rampant corruption in D.C.”

	In a clip released by Netflix, Patel jokes about Kash Patel, saying he is “the first Indian director of the FBI,” which means “he is also the last Indian director of the FBI.”
	

	“He’s too short to lead the FBI,” Patel quips. “You can’t be five-seven and in charge of finding missing people. How about you find the rest of yourself first? … Up next on Kash’s most wanted: legs.”


	The special was filmed at the Lincoln Theater in Washington, D.C., across four shows in April. It marks Patel’s one-hour stand-up debut on Netflix. Mookie Thompson directed “Buy the Dip” and executive produces alongside Patel, Daniel Powell, Alex Bach and Natalya Yonathan.

	Netflix originally licensed a different special from Patel titled “Instant Karma,” which was set to debut on April 1, 2025. But on that day, Variety reported that Netflix would not be debuting “Instant Karma,” instead ordering a brand-new special from Patel to be released in the future.

	Asked for a quote for this story about the “Buy the Dip” launch date, Patel replied, “Finally.”

	Patel’s comedy career started taking off after he was hired as a writer for Chris Rock’s 2016 Oscars hosting stint. His writing credits also include “Saturday Night Live” and the White House Correspondents Dinner. In 2023, Variety named him one of 10 Comics to Watch.

            The parents of 5-year-old Saylor Hayes have been arrested for allegedly abandoning their child, leading to her untimely death in a South Carolina river, according to police.
      
    
            Georgetown County Sheriff Carter Weaver announced Tuesday that John Herb Hayes III and Geordyn Nichole Hayes were apprehended in Carter County, Tennessee, and are currently awaiting extradition back to Georgetown.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Weaver said the two were charged with unlawfully placing a child at risk/willfully abandoning a child in connection with Saylor disappearing from a rental home in Hagley Estates on Pawleys Island, SC, and then ending up dead.
      

            Police said Hayes' body was discovered Monday morning in the Waccamaw River during an intense search for the child involving multiple agencies.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A rep for the Georgetown Sheriff's Office told TMZ ... Saylor went missing from the rental home Sunday -- and her parents called police around 11:30 AM to report that she had disappeared.
      
    
            Hundreds of people participated in the search, with agents from the Department of Natural Resources spotting Saylor's corpse floating on the water's surface while they were in a boat.
      
    
            The medical examiner is conducting an autopsy to determine Saylor's cause and manner of death.

                              September 1, 2026
                            7:20 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 2, 2026
                                6:41 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A Massachusetts woman was arrested outside the courthouse where jurors have been deliberating in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial ... though police have not said whether her arrest is connected to the popularized case.
      
    
            Dawn Light was taken into custody Tuesday around 3:40 p.m. outside Plymouth Superior Court, a Massachusetts State Police spokesperson told WCVB.
      
    
            Light is reportedly expected to face a charge of intimidating a witness, juror, or person providing information in connection with criminal proceedings.
      

            Police did not immediately provide further details or confirm whether the alleged offense involved the Clancy proceedings.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Light's arrest came just minutes after jurors were dismissed for the 4th day of deliberations. The jury had informed the judge earlier Tuesday that it was deadlocked, but was ordered to continue deliberating. Jurors are expected back in court Wednesday.
      
    
            Clancy, is currently being accused of killing her three children -- 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan -- in 2023.
      
    
            Her defense attorney Kevin Reddington has argued Clancy was suffering from postpartum psychosis and was not criminally responsible, while prosecutors contend the killings were planned.
      
    
            Clancy faces life in prison if convicted of murder.
